summary: Conover Beacon, Leonardo, NJ: front light of the Chapel Hill range, first lit 1856. Restored by Middletown and relit with a green light in 2024.

access.note: Grounds open (LighthouseFriends, before the 2022-2024 restoration). Owned by Monmouth County and managed by Middletown Township. Check with the township before going up the tower.

facts.agency: Middletown Township (manages); Monmouth County (owner, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Hexagonal wooden tower and wooden keeper's dwelling built by Richard Calrow Jr.
First lit as the front light of the Chapel Hill range.
Board reported the tower frail and shaky; funds for repair reverted to the Treasury.
Black daymark screens, 25 ft high and 20 ft wide, set on either side of the tower.
Wire fence and 162 ft of plank drain built through the reservation.
Oil house built at the front beacon.
Light discontinued 28 April to 1 August 1898 as a safety measure during the Spanish-American War.
Illuminant changed from mineral oil to incandescent oil vapor, 20 January 1907.
Range lights discontinued in July 1923 when gas-lighted buoys marked the channel.
Range lights reactivated about four months later after tugboat captains complained.
Concrete-block saw-tooth jetty placed along the shore to protect the reservation.
Current metal tower, 45 ft, replaced the hexagonal wooden tower. It was the front light of the Waackaack range, moved from Point Comfort, Keansburg.
Official use ended in 1957 per LighthouseFriends and the Two River Times.
Deactivated per the township; TRT says a lightkeeper maintained and lit it until 1988.
Transferred to Monmouth County for management by Middletown Township.
Hurricane Sandy damaged the base of the tower.
Green solar light after sunset, because the light is decommissioned.

corrections.why: The record merges two towers. The 1856 tower was wood, and the 13.7 m (45 ft) steel tower is the 1941 replacement.
LighthouseFriends, the USLHS record and the township all date the replacement tower to 1941.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and the Two River Times date the end of official use to 1957. The township gives 1988, and TRT says a lightkeeper lit the light until 1988. The story gives both dates and does not choose.
The USLHS roster begins in 1855 with Mark L. Mount; USLHS establishment, LighthouseFriends and the township give 1856. The story uses 1856.

notes_for_editor: (1) Two end dates: 1957 (LighthouseFriends; TRT official use) against 1988 (township; Wikipedia lead only). The record's 'deactivated 1988' follows the township. (2) TRT says a lightkeeper maintained and lit the light from 1957 to 1988, but the USLHS roster ends in 1923 and LighthouseFriends says inactive from 1957. The staffing entry uses the roster date (1923). (3) Keeper names: 'Mark' (USLHS) against 'Marsh' (LighthouseFriends) Mount; 'Ernest Bloom' against 'Ernest R. Bloom'. (4) First lit: USLHS roster starts 1855; establishment and township give 1856. (5) A 1903 Jersey City News list (OCR) gives the tower as 'more than fifty-seven feet'; LighthouseFriends and the township give 55 ft. Not used. (6) Ownership: LighthouseFriends says Monmouth County owns it; the township treats it as its own and says it manages it. (7) Access: USLHS says not open to the public, LighthouseFriends (undated, before restoration) says grounds open and tower closed. Whether the tower may be climbed now is not stated in the township page or TRT; the mayor says the stairs are now safe. Check before publishing any climbing advice. (8) The 1868 Board report and the Kobbe 1889 description are second-hand, quoted by LighthouseFriends. Neither the 1868 report nor Kobbe was in the local corpus. (9) Wikipedia was used for leads only; its references (NPS inventory, Coast Guard historian pages, New Jersey Lighthouse Society) were not read. (10) The 1894 keeper item is a newspaper social note. Keeper Foster's identity is confirmed by the roster line and the 1900 item. (11) The 1892 Board report passage is cited by scan page 634; the printed page is not confirmed. The 1895 corpus OCR reads 'Gonover beacon (front)'; checked as the Conover front beacon. The 1895 entry is quoted by scan page 249. (12) The 1900 Monmouth Inquirer item reads 'Tne keeper of the beacon is S. A. Foster' in OCR; quoted as printed. (13) No wrecks or rescues tied to this light were found in the sources read, so no wrecks key was written. (14) Record corrections: the record merges the 1856 wooden tower and the 1941 steel tower, and it dates Tower 2 to 1926 (Rowlett's) where the 1941 date is the sourced one. (15) No photos mirrored. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28 (Haiku 5.5): checked each footnoted sentence against the cached sources and corpus pages. Confirmed: 1892 Board report scan 634 (the detour, the range-light sentence, 'obscured by mist or smoke', and the night passage, with a width of about 900 feet between buoys); 1894 report scan 379 (wire fence and 162 feet of plank drain, Conover front beacon, entry 293); 1895 report scan 249 (entry 301, 'Gonover beacon (front)', oil house; the OCR misreads the C as G); Monmouth Inquirer 11 January 1894 and 27 December 1900 (both read on the cached pages). Corrections in the story: 'Lighthouse Service roster' is now the U.S. Lighthouse Society's; the 1856 daymark sentence now says LighthouseFriends calls the red-band daymark the one used today (it had contradicted the 1874 and 1901 screens); the iron guys are no longer linked to the settling by 'so'; funds 'authorized' rather than 'voted'; the township page's 45-foot figure now carries metres; the ownership statement is attributed to LighthouseFriends, which predates the restoration; the 'Before going up' advice is replaced by a plain statement that no source says whether the public may climb the tower now, with the USLHS 'Open to Public: No' and LighthouseFriends' pre-restoration 'tower closed'. The mayor's remark is quoted from The Two River Times, not from the township. Unresolved: the end of official use (1957 against 1988, see resolved_conflicts).
